title: Leaving Canada? What happens to your taxes
seo_title: Leaving Canada: Tax Guide for Emigrants and Departure Tax
description: Becoming a non-resident, your final return, departure tax, T1161 and T1244, withholding on Canadian income, and what happens to your RRSP, TFSA and FHSA.
lead: Moving abroad changes how Canada taxes you, and the year you leave has its own rules and forms. Here's what to sort out before and after you go.
key_points: You become a non-resident when you cut your residential ties, usually on the latest of when you leave, when your family leaves, or when you become resident elsewhere.
Your final return reports world income up to your departure date and only certain Canadian income after it.
Most property is treated as sold at market value when you leave, but Canadian real estate and registered plans like RRSPs and TFSAs are not.
File Form T1161 if your property is worth over $25,000; you can defer departure tax with Form T1244.
After you leave, Canadian payers usually withhold 25% on income like rent, pensions and RRSP withdrawals, unless a treaty lowers it.
Stop TFSA contributions once you are a non-resident, and repay any HBP or LLP balance within 60 days of leaving.

sections.heading: When you stop being a Canadian resident
sections.html:
Canada taxes people based on residency, not citizenship. You become an emigrant for tax when you leave Canada to live in another country and cut your residential ties, the links between your life and Canada.

  • Significant ties: a home in Canada, a spouse or common-law partner in Canada, and dependants in Canada.
  • Secondary ties: personal property such as a car or furniture, social ties, economic ties such as bank accounts and credit cards, a Canadian driver's licence, and provincial health insurance.

Cutting ties usually means selling or giving up your Canadian home, setting up a permanent home abroad, having your spouse and children move too, and moving your personal and social life to the new country.

Three ways the CRA may see you

StatusWhat it means
Factual residentYou live or work abroad but keep significant ties here, such as a home or family in Canada. You are still treated as a resident of Canada for tax.
Deemed non-residentYou still have ties to Canada, but under a tax treaty you are a resident of the other country. You are treated like an emigrant.
Non-resident (emigrant)You have cut your significant ties. Canada taxes only certain Canadian income.

A separate rule can make a person a deemed resident: someone without significant ties who stays in Canada for 183 days or more in a year.

If your situation is unclear, you can ask the CRA for its opinion using Form NR73, Determination of Residency Status (leaving Canada). It is optional.

sections.heading: Your departure date
sections.html:
Your departure date is the day you become a non-resident. It is usually the latest of these dates:

  • the day you leave Canada;
  • the day your spouse or common-law partner and dependants leave Canada;
  • the day you become a resident of your new country.

Example: you fly to your new country on June 1, but your spouse and children stay to finish the school year and join you on July 15. Your departure date is usually July 15.

Exception: if you lived in another country before and are going back there, you generally become a non-resident on the day you leave, even if your spouse stays behind for a while to sell your home.

If you don't need to file a return for the year you leave, still tell the CRA your departure date as soon as you can.

sections.heading: Your final (departure-year) tax return
sections.html:
In the year you leave, you file a return that covers two periods, with your departure date on page 1. Use the BC forms if you lived in BC on your departure date.

  • Before you left: report your world income (Canadian and foreign) in Canadian dollars.
  • After you left: report only certain Canadian income, such as pay for work done in Canada. Other Canadian income, like interest and rent, is usually handled by withholding at source (see below).

Credits and deductions

  • Your federal non-refundable credits, such as the basic personal amount, are generally limited to the part of the year you were a resident. BC credits may be limited too.
  • Most deductions still apply. Moving expenses for a move abroad generally aren't deductible, except for certain full-time students.
  • BC refundable credits are generally not available unless you were a resident on December 31.

Due dates

The return is due April 30 of the year after you leave, or June 15 if you or your spouse carried on a business. Any balance owing is due by April 30 either way. For example, if you leave in 2026, the usual deadline is April 30, 2027.

sections.heading: Departure tax: the deemed sale of your property
sections.html:
When you leave, the CRA treats you as if you sold most of your property at its fair market value (FMV), the price it would fetch on the open market, on your departure date, and bought it straight back. This is a deemed disposition, often called "departure tax." You pay tax on any gain even though you sold nothing.

Example: you bought shares in a non-registered account for $20,000 and they are worth $50,000 when you leave. You report a $30,000 capital gain on your final return.

Property that is not deemed sold

  • Canadian real estate, such as your house, condo or rental property, and Canadian resource and timber property. It stays taxable in Canada when you actually sell it later.
  • Property of a business you carry on through a permanent establishment in Canada.
  • Registered plans and pensions: RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, RESPs, RDSPs, pension plans, annuities, most employee stock options taxed in Canada, and Canadian life insurance (other than segregated funds).
  • Short-term residents: if you lived in Canada for 60 months or less in the 10 years before leaving, property you owned when you last arrived (or inherited after arriving) is not deemed sold.

The forms

  • Form T1243 calculates the gains and losses from the deemed sale. You then report them on Schedule 3 of your return.
  • Form T1161, the list of properties, is required if the FMV of everything you own is more than $25,000 when you leave. Leave out cash and bank deposits, registered plans, and personal-use items (household goods, clothing, cars) worth under $10,000. It is due by your filing due date even if you don't otherwise need to file a return. The late-filing penalty is $25 a day, at least $100 and up to $2,500.

Deferring the tax: Form T1244

You can choose to put off paying departure tax until you actually sell the property, with no interest, by filing Form T1244 by April 30 of the year after you leave. If the federal tax you are deferring is more than $16,500, you must give the CRA adequate security (a guarantee of payment), and you may need security for provincial tax too. Contact the CRA before April 30 to arrange it.

Get values on your departure date. Save statements and valuations showing what each investment was worth the day you left. If you later move back, you may be able to elect to undo the deemed sale on property you still own, and you will need these numbers.

sections.heading: Canadian income after you leave
sections.html:
Withholding tax (Part XIII)

Once you are a non-resident, Canadian payers must hold back non-resident tax (called Part XIII tax) on income such as dividends, rent, pensions, OAS, CPP, RRSP and RRIF payments and annuities. The usual rate is 25%, unless a tax treaty between Canada and your new country lowers it. You get an NR4 slip showing what was paid and withheld. This is usually your final Canadian tax on that income, so you generally don't file a return for it.

The section 217 election

If most of your income is Canadian pension-type income, such as CPP, OAS, workplace pensions, RRSP or RRIF payments, or EI, you can choose to file a Canadian return under section 217. You are then taxed at normal resident rates and may get back some or all of the 25% withheld. The CRA only applies the election if it helps you, and the return must be filed on time.

Keeping a Canadian rental property

  • Your tenant or property manager must withhold 25% of the gross rent and send it to the CRA.
  • With an approved Form NR6, filed with a Canadian agent (a resident who acts for you) on or before January 1 each year or before the first rent payment is due, the 25% is withheld on the net rent (rent minus expenses) instead.
  • Under section 216 you can file a separate return for your rental income to pay tax on the net profit and get back extra tax withheld. If you used an NR6, you file this return by June 30 of the next year. Without an NR6, you generally have two years from the end of the year to file it.

Selling Canadian property later

When a non-resident sells taxable Canadian property, such as Canadian real estate, you must tell the CRA within 10 days of the sale (or before a proposed sale) using Form T2062, along with payment or security for the tax. The CRA then issues a certificate of compliance. Without one, the buyer may hold back 25% of the price (50% for some property). Late notice costs $25 a day, at least $100 and up to $2,500. You must also file a return for the year of sale by April 30 of the next year.

sections.heading: Your RRSP, TFSA, FHSA, HBP and LLP
sections.html:
AccountWhat happens when you leave
RRSP / RRIFNot deemed sold. You can keep it. Withdrawals after you leave have 25% non-resident tax withheld (less if a treaty applies). A section 217 election may lower the tax.
TFSAYou can keep it, and its income and withdrawals aren't taxed in Canada. No new room builds for any full year you are a non-resident. Withdrawals are added back to your room only if you become a resident again.
FHSAYou can keep it, but you can't make a tax-free qualifying withdrawal for a home while you are a non-resident. Taxable withdrawals have 25% withheld, unless a treaty lowers it.
Home Buyers' Plan (HBP)Repay the remaining balance by the earlier of when you file your return for the year you leave, or 60 days after you become a non-resident. Anything not repaid is added to that year's income.
Lifelong Learning Plan (LLP)Same deadline: repay the balance, or it is added to your income for the year you leave.
Don't contribute to your TFSA after you leave. A contribution made while you are a non-resident is taxed at 1% for each month it stays in the account, until you withdraw it or move back. Your new country may also tax TFSA income, so check its rules.

sections.heading: Benefits, banks and other loose ends
sections.html:
• Benefits stop. As a non-resident you are generally not eligible for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit or the Canada child benefit (or related provincial payments such as the B.C. family benefit). Tell the CRA your departure date. If payments keep arriving after you leave, contact the CRA right away.
  • Tell your banks and payers. Let every Canadian bank, brokerage, pension plan and other payer know you are now a non-resident, so they withhold the right tax and issue NR4 slips.
  • Update your address with the CRA and keep access to My Account. You will still need it for NR4 slips, rental returns and correspondence.
  • Keep records of your departure date, property values and returns for at least six years.

sections.heading: Checklist before and after you leave
sections.html:
1. Decide your departure date and keep proof (tickets, lease or sale documents, new-country residence papers).
  2. Consider whether you are cutting your ties; use NR73 if you want the CRA's view.
  3. Get the fair market value of investments and other property on your departure date.
  4. Complete T1243 and, if your property is worth over $25,000, T1161.
  5. Decide whether to defer departure tax with T1244 (by April 30 of the next year), and arrange security if federal tax is over $16,500.
  6. Repay any HBP or LLP balance within 60 days of leaving, or plan for the tax.
  7. Stop TFSA contributions from your departure date.
  8. If you keep a rental, appoint a Canadian agent and file NR6 before rent starts.
  9. Tell the CRA, your banks and other payers that you are a non-resident.
  10. File your final return by April 30 of the year after you leave.

Leaving Canada with investments, a home or registered plans involves several one-time decisions, and a tax professional can help you plan them before you go.
